checklist.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Is deposit request ordering deterministically derived from receipt_keys order across all EL implementations?

reachability.notes: A malicious block producer controls receipt ordering. If EL implementations use different key ordering, they will produce different deposit sequences and different requests hashes.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Identify all code paths that iterate over receipt_keys to extract deposit requests. 2. Verify that the iteration order is deterministic and matches the canonical receipt_keys ordering in block_output. 3. Create test blocks with multiple deposit events from different transactions and verify consistent ordering across EL client implementations. 4. Specifically test edge cases: (a) deposits in same transaction but different log indices, (b) deposits across transactions with adjacent indices, (c) maximum number of deposits in a block. 5. Compare the resulting deposit_requests sequences and requests hashes between at least two different EL implementations (e.g., Geth, Nethermind, Besu, Erigon). 6. Attempt to craft a block where ambiguous key ordering could cause divergence.
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0016, Trust Boundaries: tb-003, tb-004, Invariant: SG-002/INV-008, Threat: stride-006

checklist.title: Verify Block Producer Cannot Manipulate Deposit Order: Are receipt_keys validated against the canonical ordering before processing?

reachability.notes: A malicious block producer controls receipt ordering. If EL implementations use different key ordering, they will produce different deposit sequences and different requests hashes.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Review how receipt_keys are derived or provided in block_output. 2. Verify that receipt_keys are sorted using a consistent, deterministic comparison function (e.g., lexicographic byte ordering). 3. Test that a malicious block producer cannot supply receipt_keys in a non-canonical order that would still be accepted. 4. Attempt to submit blocks with receipt_keys in different orderings (reverse, random, partially sorted) and verify rejection or normalization. 5. Check that the receipt trie iteration produces keys in the same order as the expected canonical ordering.
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0016, Trust Boundary: tb-003 (Block Producer to EL Node), Assumption: asm-007

checklist.title: Verify Requests Hash Changes with Deposit Reordering: Does swapping deposit order produce a detectably different requests hash?

reachability.notes: A malicious block producer controls receipt ordering. If EL implementations use different key ordering, they will produce different deposit sequences and different requests hashes.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Create two test scenarios with identical deposit data but different orderings. 2. Compute the requests hash for each ordering and verify they differ. 3. Verify that the hash function is order-sensitive (i.e., no accidental use of a commutative operation like XOR). 4. Trace through the hash computation to confirm deposits are processed sequentially in list order. 5. Create a falsification test: attempt to find two different orderings that produce the same hash (this should be impossible with correct implementation).
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0016, Supporting internal verification for the boundary property

checklist.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Does the deposit_requests accumulator concatenate valid deposit data without gaps or reordering?

reachability.notes: If deposit concatenation skips entries or introduces padding, the resulting requests hash will differ between implementations.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Identify the deposit_requests accumulator implementation in the EL client codebase. 2. Trace the code path from receipt processing to deposit concatenation. 3. Verify that deposits are appended sequentially without padding bytes or alignment gaps. 4. Test with multiple deposits in a single block to ensure no reordering occurs. 5. Compare the concatenation output against the reference implementation (ethereum/execution-specs). 6. Create test cases with edge cases: (a) single deposit, (b) multiple deposits from same transaction, (c) deposits spanning multiple transactions, (d) maximum deposits per block. 7. Verify that the final deposit_requests byte array equals concat(extract_deposit_data(log.data) for each matching log in receipt_keys order) with no extra bytes.
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0017, Trust Boundary: tb-002, Invariant: SG-002/INV-009. Gap or reordering in deposit accumulation would cause requests hash mismatch between EL implementations, leading to consensus split. Attacker can control deposit events via transactions, making this externally exploitable.

checklist.title: Verify Deposit Accumulator Byte-Level Correctness: Are deposit data bytes concatenated exactly as specified without additional encoding or padding?

reachability.notes: If deposit concatenation skips entries or introduces padding, the resulting requests hash will differ between implementations.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Review the deposit_requests byte array construction code. 2. Verify that each extract_deposit_data result (192 bytes) is appended directly without length prefixes, delimiters, or padding. 3. Test with deposits of varying counts and verify total length equals count * 192 bytes. 4. Check for any memory alignment operations that might introduce gaps (e.g., struct padding in C/Go). 5. Hex-dump the deposit_requests output and compare byte-by-byte with expected concatenation. 6. Test cross-implementation: generate deposit_requests in one EL client and verify byte-exact match in another.
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0017, Supporting boundary check. Incorrect byte-level concatenation (extra length bytes, alignment padding) would cause hash mismatch.

checklist.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Is receipt trie lookup failure properly handled with block rejection?

reachability.notes: A malicious block producer can craft a block where the receipts trie is inconsistent with receipt_keys, causing trie_get to return None.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Identify the code path where trie_get is called with receipt_keys from block_output. 2. Trace what happens when trie_get returns None for a key: Does it raise an exception, return an error, or silently continue? 3. Craft a test block where receipts_trie is missing an entry for one of the receipt_keys. 4. Submit this malformed block via P2P and observe behavior: Does the node crash (DoS vulnerability), panic, or properly reject with InvalidBlock? 5. Verify that all code paths handling None results terminate with block rejection. 6. Check for null pointer dereferences or unhandled None cases that could cause crashes.
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0018, Trust Boundary: tb-003, Pre-condition: trie_get must return non-None for all receipt_keys, Invariant: SG-002/INV-010, Assumption: asm-014, Threat: stride-017. Severity justified by potential for node crashes causing network split between crashing and non-crashing implementations.

checklist.title: Verify Block Producer Cannot Cause Node Crash via Inconsistent Receipt Trie

reachability.notes: A malicious block producer can craft a block where the receipts trie is inconsistent with receipt_keys, causing trie_get to return None.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Review the block producer trust boundary (tb-003) and identify all data paths from block producer to EL node. 2. Enumerate all ways a malicious block producer can create inconsistency between receipts_trie and receipt_keys: a) Missing trie entries, b) Corrupted trie structure, c) Invalid keys in receipt_keys list. 3. For each inconsistency type, create a test case and verify the EL node rejects the block without crashing. 4. Verify consistent behavior across multiple EL implementations to ensure no consensus divergence. 5. Check error handling code for memory safety issues (Go: nil dereference, C++: null pointer access). 6. Confirm that InvalidBlock is raised before any state changes occur.
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0018, Supporting check for actor-block-producer and actor-el-node interaction. Focus on ensuring malicious block producers cannot exploit trie inconsistencies.

checklist.title: Falsification Test: Can trie_get return None without triggering InvalidBlock rejection?

reachability.notes: A malicious block producer can craft a block where the receipts trie is inconsistent with receipt_keys, causing trie_get to return None.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Design a falsification test that attempts to violate the pre-condition: find a code path where trie_get returns None but the block is not rejected. 2. Instrument the trie_get function to track all call sites and return values. 3. For each call site, verify that a None return is immediately followed by an InvalidBlock exception or equivalent error propagation. 4. Search for any catch blocks or error suppression that might swallow the None case. 5. Test with fuzz inputs: generate random combinations of receipts_trie and receipt_keys to find edge cases. 6. Verify that the pre-condition holds: forall (key in receipt_keys): trie_get(receipts_trie, key) != None OR block is rejected.
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0018, Formal verification approach to validate the pre-condition. This check attempts to falsify the property by finding any code path that violates it.

checklist.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Is the double-SHA-256 hash construction correctly implemented in compute_requests_hash?

reachability.notes: This is an implementation correctness property. An incorrect implementation (single SHA-256 vs double SHA-256) would cause consensus divergence between any two implementations that differ.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Locate the compute_requests_hash function in the EL client codebase. 2. Verify the hash construction follows the specified double-SHA-256 pattern: for each request, compute sha256(request).digest(), then update an outer sha256 hasher with each individual digest. 3. Confirm the construction produces sha256(sha256(r1) || sha256(r2) || ...) NOT sha256(r1 || r2 || ...). 4. Create test vectors with known requests and compute expected hashes manually using the double-SHA-256 construction. 5. Verify the implementation produces the correct output for all test vectors. 6. Attempt to falsify by comparing against single SHA-256 construction (sha256(r1 || r2)) and confirming outputs differ. 7. Cross-check against reference implementations from other EL clients (Geth, Nethermind, Besu, Erigon) to ensure hash compatibility. 8. Verify edge cases: empty requests list, single request, requests of varying lengths.
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0019, Trust Boundary: tb-004 (EL/CL interface), Invariant: SG-003/INV-011, Assumption: asm-008, Threat: stride-019. Critical for cross-client consensus - incorrect hash construction would cause deterministic network split.

checklist.title: Falsification Test: Can compute_requests_hash produce inconsistent results across EL implementations?

reachability.notes: This is an implementation correctness property. An incorrect implementation (single SHA-256 vs double SHA-256) would cause consensus divergence between any two implementations that differ.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Design a cross-client test suite to falsify the invariant: find any input that produces different hashes across EL implementations. 2. Generate diverse test cases: (a) empty requests, (b) single small request, (c) multiple requests, (d) maximum-size requests, (e) requests with special byte patterns (all zeros, all ones, boundary values). 3. For each test case, compute the requests hash using at least two different EL client implementations. 4. Compare hash outputs byte-for-byte to detect any divergence. 5. If divergence is found, trace through both implementations to identify which one deviates from the spec. 6. Verify the spec interpretation: confirm both implementations agree on the double-SHA-256 construction semantics. 7. Test with Hive or similar cross-client testing framework for automated comparison.
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0019, Formal verification approach to detect cross-client hash computation inconsistencies. This is a critical check for preventing network splits.

checklist.title: Verify Trust Boundary Integrity: Does compute_requests_hash maintain strict request ordering during hash computation?

reachability.notes: Order-dependency of the hash means implementations must agree on request ordering. Different orderings produce different hashes.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Locate the compute_requests_hash function in the EL client codebase. 2. Verify that the iteration order over the requests list is deterministic and follows list index order. 3. Confirm that requests are processed in the exact order they appear in the input list (index 0 first, then index 1, etc.). 4. Check for any sorting, shuffling, or parallel processing that could alter iteration order. 5. Create test with multiple requests [r1, r2, r3] and verify hash([r1, r2, r3]) != hash([r2, r1, r3]) != hash([r3, r2, r1]). 6. Examine any concurrent or async operations that might affect order (e.g., goroutines in Go, async iterators). 7. Cross-check hash output against reference implementation for identical request ordering. 8. Test edge cases: (a) duplicate requests at different positions should produce different hashes if swapped, (b) single-element list, (c) large lists at boundary sizes.
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0020, Trust Boundary: tb-004 (EL/CL interface), Invariant: SG-003/INV-012, Assumption: asm-008, Threat: stride-007. Different request ordering across EL implementations would produce different hashes, causing consensus divergence and network split.

checklist.title: Falsification Test: Can swapped request ordering produce identical hash in compute_requests_hash?

reachability.notes: Order-dependency of the hash means implementations must agree on request ordering. Different orderings produce different hashes.

checklist.test_procedure: 1. Design a falsification test that attempts to violate the invariant: find two different orderings of the same requests that produce the same hash. 2. Generate test cases with at least two distinct requests r1 and r2 where r1 != r2. 3. Compute hash([r1, r2]) and hash([r2, r1]) and verify they differ. 4. Check for accidental use of commutative operations in the hash construction (e.g., XOR instead of concatenation). 5. Search for any code paths where ordering information is lost before hashing. 6. Verify that the hash function is not using set-based or order-invariant data structures. 7. Test with requests that have similar byte patterns to ensure the hash is truly order-sensitive. 8. Confirm the mathematical property holds: forall (r1, r2 where r1 != r2): hash([r1, r2]) != hash([r2, r1]).
checklist.notes: Source: PROP-0020, Formal verification approach to validate the ordering invariant. This check attempts to falsify the property by finding any ordering that produces a hash collision.
